en: The Garland of Logical Connections (Śārīrakīyā Nayasaṅgatimālikā)
Composed by Śrīnivāsācārya at Lakṣmīpura.
I take refuge in the infinite, true, blissful, and stainless consciousness, the cause of all worlds and the shelter for those who have taken refuge in it.
Having paid homage to the most noble succession of my own gurus, I compose this *Nayasaṅgatimālikā* on the established tenets of the *Śrībhāṣya*.

Connection (*saṅgati*) is considered to be the relationship between the object of the knowledge that serves as the cause for the inquiry that is prompted when [a topic] is mentioned immediately after [another]. (1)
Connection, introduction, exception, counter-example, illustration, objection, extended application, and incidental discussion: thus [the connection] is sevenfold. (2)
The introduction (upoddhāta): An introduction is that which serves as a supporting factor for the subject matter at hand;
the wise know an introduction to be a reflection intended for the successful accomplishment of the topic under discussion. (3)
An exception (apavāda) relies upon the logic of the established conclusion (siddhānta) of the preceding section;
it is the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) for the subsequent section, and therein it functions as an exception.
A counter-example (*pratyudāhṛti*) occurs when,
having taken as its basis the fact that a previously established principle (*siddhāntanyāya*) does not apply to the current case,
a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is raised. (5)

An example (dṛṣ�ṭānta) arises from reliance upon similarity with a previously established topic, a settled tenet (siddhānta), or a logical principle (nyāya); its application occurs when a subsequent topic is introduced. (6)

An objection (ākṣepa) consists in suspecting the untenability of the logic of the established conclusion (siddhānta) under discussion; when the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) arises from such a suspicion, there is the connection known as "objection" (ākṣepasaṅgati).
When, having raised a further doubt, that which was previously extended [by analogy] is itself further extended,
the wise call that a certain type of "extension" (atideśika) as a point of connection (saṅgati).
A *prasaṅga* (a consequential argument) consists in the unsuitability of indifference [to a point] because of its connection with a previously mentioned subject.
As for what they call a *prasaṅga*, it is indeed a form of *saṅgati* (logical coherence).

Therefore, the definition of *prasaṅga* (an incidental discussion) is extracted as follows: that connection which is distinct from the connections based on introduction (*upodghāta*) and so forth is *prasaṅga*; this is the isolated definition. || 10 ||

For in this work, the connection [between sections] is generally indicated by means of specific notices such as the word "exception" (apavāda) and so forth; let the learned grasp this as a general principle. (11)

The primary subjects of the three sections [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra] consist of: dharma, cognition, the divisions of the means of knowledge, the subsidiaries, application, order, the agent, extension (atideśa), particularity (viśeṣa), sublation (bādha), the general framework (tantra), and incidental connection (prasaṅga). || 12 ||
In the section concerning the deities (devatākāṇḍa), the essential nature of the deities, their distinctions, the preliminary worship thereof, and the resulting fruit are all described.
Consistency, non-contradiction, the means of proof, and the purpose—these are the primary subjects within the twenty characteristics across the three sections. (14)
This third section, consisting of two pairs [of chapters], contains internal subdivisions of the *Śarīra*.
Its subject matter is twofold—as that which is established (*siddha*) and that which is to be established (*sādhya*)—and likewise as the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*). (15)

In this *Śārīraka*, the connections (*saṅgati*) are to be considered through the divisions of the treatise (*śāstra*), the sections (*kāṇḍa*), the chapters (*adhyāya*), the sub-sections (*peṭikā*), the topics (*adhikaraṇa*), and the feet (*pāda*). Furthermore, the connection here must be stated as eightfold according to the distinctions among the sūtras.

In this context, the connection within the six categories, such as the treatise and so forth, consists in being included [within them]; furthermore, the connection between the qualification and the aphorism should be understood as consisting in immediate succession. (17)
Because it consists of the principles of the meaning of the Vedas, there is a connection with the Mīmāṃsā system;
because it is an inquiry into the meaning of the Vedānta, its connection with this specific section (kāṇḍa) is stated. (18)
Because it is an inquiry into an already established reality, it is connected with the first pair [of chapters];
because its primary focus is on reconciliation (samanvaya), it is connected with the first chapter. || 19 ||
The division of the commentary on the first chapter:
In this chapter, "Exclusion of Non-Connection," there shall be three sections (peṭikā), according to the sequence of four, three, and four principles (naya). (20)
The purpose of the first section:
First, let it be understood that this first section establishes the non-commencement of the treatise by means of four logical arguments. (21)

The introductory section [is as follows]: For it is stated in the final topic of the Devatākāṇḍa: "Because he is seen at the end [of the Upanishads] as Hari, therefore he is Viṣṇu"; and after this [it continues]: 23.

Because it is designated by the term "Brahman" and so forth, it falls within the scope of the meaning of the word "Brahman"; therefore, [the author] refutes its lack of renown, and thus there is a logical connection through this objection. || 25 ||
Thus ends the section on the desire to know (Jijñāsā-adhikaraṇa). || 1 ||

Since it is established that the existence of an object is proven by means of the definitions of the instruments of valid cognition, the examination of the objects of cognition (prameya) follows, being rooted in the critique of those very instruments of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 26 ||
Thus ends the section concerning "origination and so forth" (Janmādyadhikaraṇa). || 2 ||

Since it is impossible for [the existence of] God, established through inference, to be attained [through scripture], the objection regarding the authority [of scripture] was raised and refuted in the section on "Scripture as the Source" (Śāstrayoni-adhikaraṇa). || 27 ||
Thus concludes the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] entitled "Having Scripture as its Source" (Śāstrayonitva). 3.

The fourth method, that of systematic coordination (samanvaya), severed the objection to [the Veda's] authority by eliminating the pervasive [defects] within the sequence of [the opponent's] efforts to produce the fruits of life. || 28 ||

The impossibility of a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) due to the non-establishment of the object to be defined (lakṣya)—that which is a lack of connection—is what is expressed in the first quarter [of the verse] as its exclusion. (29)
In brief, the distinction is this: over-extension (*ativyāpti*) is the connection with something else; its exclusion constitutes the meaning of the three quarters [of the verse]. (30)
Thus concludes the section on Concordance (Samanvayādhikaraṇa).
The *Catussūtrī* has been completed;

it declares that the true knowledge which is the essence of the Vedānta holds that primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is the cause. Now follows the refutation of this objection according to the principle of "seeing" (*īkṣati*). (31)
Thus, many types of conjunctions have been described according to their various distinctions;
therein, the primary one has been summarized for the sake of pacifying the disciple's distraction.
Thus ends the section concerning "Iksati" (The One who Sees). 5.
Now, in the section concerning Ānanda, the objection that the individual soul (jīva), being characterized by primary seeing and so forth, might be the cause of the world, is here refuted. (33)
Thus concludes the section concerning that which consists of bliss (Ānandamaya-adhikaraṇa).
By the scriptural text "He who is this," as a supplement to the preceding section, the status of the merit and the individual soul as causes is internally sublated.
Thus ends the section concerning the intermediate state (antaradhikaraṇa). 7.
A specific indicative mark (liṅga) is considered stronger than a general scriptural statement (śruti);
since the opposite is the case here regarding the principle of ether (ākāśa), this is cited as a counter-example.
Thus ends the section concerning ether (ākāśādhikaraṇa). 8.
Having raised a further doubt here, [the author] refutes it by extending the previous reasoning;
thus, in the *Prāṇanaya*, the connection is one of extension (*ātideśika*). (36)
Thus ends the section concerning the vital breath (prāṇa). 9.
Because no specific marks of Brahman mentioned in its own [preceding] statement are observed here, light (jyotis) is investigated; therefore, there is a connection by way of a counter-example.
Thus ends the section concerning light (Jyotir-adhikaraṇa). 10.
The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) arises from what was stated previously, based on the force of the opening statement;
however, in the section concerning Indra and Prāṇa, the connection is one of exception (āpavādika).
Thus, in the first quarter of the first chapter,
there are three sections (peṭikās) as well as eleven topics (adhikaraṇas).
Section 11: The Topic of Indra and Prāṇa.
Now, in this second chapter, there are two sections: the Section on Worship consisting of the abidings in small stations and great stations, divided into groups of three and two. (40)
The mark of Brahman contained within the Great Sayings (mahāvākya) is declared to be powerful;
through such a mark, doubt is dispelled in every philosophical system.
Thus ends the section [concerning] the universal establishment [of Brahman]. 1.

If there is no state of being an enjoyer for the Inner Controller, then that [Inner Controller] must be the individual soul (jīva) itself; because of this doubt regarding the "eater" (attā), the present section is introduced as a counter-example. || 42 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the eater (Atrādhikaraṇa). 2.
In the context of being difficult to see, [the Lord] is "Sudarśana" (Beautiful to Behold) because He is visible to the eyes;
then, through the connection of providing a counter-example, there arises the introduction of another topic. 43.
Thus concludes the section on the intermediate state.

The section concerning the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmi-Adhikaraṇa) serves to establish that the person situated within the eye is indeed Brahman; therefore, it possesses the connection of being an introductory elaboration (upoddhāta-saṅgati). || 44 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin). 4.

In the section concerning "the invisible" (adṛśyatvādhikaraṇa), because the status of being the seer and so forth was not mentioned, there arose the doubt that it might be either primordial matter (prakṛti) or the individual soul (puruṣa); therefore, this counter-example is provided.
Thus ends the section [concerning] the one whose qualities are invisibility and so forth. 5.
Previously, the presentation of the Universal Form was made by means of its having heaven as its head and so forth;
now, by way of that arrangement, the Vaiśvānara-vidyā is considered as an exception to that [previous teaching]. (46)
Thus, the six topics of qualification, characterized by two sections, are well-integrated within the second quarter of the first chapter. (47)
Thus concludes the section concerning Vaiśvānara. 6.
Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter.
Then, in the third section, there is a set of four boxes according to the sequence of two, four, three, and one methods. (48)

The relationship between heaven, earth, and so forth was previously established at the end of the [third] quarter; by means of the exception that this exists in the individual soul (jīva), the determination regarding the leading [of the soul] to heaven, earth, and so on is made. (49)
Thus concludes the section concerning "Heaven, Earth, and so forth" (1).
Precisely because the subject matter of the section has been stated as being one, the arguments for the established conclusion have been proven;
thus, the exception raised in the *Bhūman* section has here been refuted by means of the individual soul (*jīva*).
Thus ends the section concerning the "Fullness" (Bhūma). 2.
This establishment of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa in their own majesty has been declared; through this negation [of other doctrines], there arises the system of the Imperishable (Akṣara). || 51 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the Imperishable (Akṣarādhikaraṇa). 3.

Since the previously mentioned "seeing of the unseen" does not apply here, this constitutes a counter-example in the section concerning the object of the act of seeing (Īkṣatikarmādhikaraṇa). || 52 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the object of the act of seeing (Īkṣatikarmādhikaraṇa). 4.
The Person dwelling within the city has been determined previously through the power of the scriptural texts concerning Puruṣa;
now, the commencement of the section on the "Small" (dahara) arises by way of connection with a counter-example.
Thus ends the section concerning the "Small" (dahara) [space]. 5.
"Let there be a limited size for Brahman when it is the subject of a specific measurement;
however, in response to this, it is argued that the individual soul (jīva) must be [the referent] because of specific scriptural statements concerning it. (54)
Thus ends the section concerning that which has been measured (the *pramitādhikaraṇa*). 6.
If it is argued that meditation (upāsana) pertains only to human beings because of the statement [in scripture] regarding "those who have measured" (pramita),
then the denial of the eligibility of gods is refuted by the method concerning the deities (devatānaya).
Thus concludes the section concerning the deities (Devatādhikaraṇa). 7.
Even if the possibility of [the application of] capacity and so forth might exist in the case of meditative worship in general,
the application of the Madhu-ādi rule occurs as a counter-example.
Thus ends the section concerning honey (Madhu-adhikaraṇa). || 8 ||

"A Śūdra may be entitled to the study of knowledge because of his possession of capability and desire"—it is for the purpose of refuting such a doubt that the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning those who are not Śūdras) arises. (57)
Thus concludes the section concerning those who are not Śūdras (Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa). 9.

Thus, by means of the method of "another meaning" (arthāntaranyāsa), [the author] has severed the exception raised by the logic of "burning," namely the fourfold set of qualifications that followed as a consequence of what preceded.
Thus ends the section concerning the designation of being a different entity and so forth. 10.
This third quarter of the first chapter, consisting of four sections and ten topics, is well-concluded. (59)
Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter.
In the fourth quarter of the first chapter, he formulated the eightfold system of logic (*nītyaṣṭaka*);
therein, by means of six methods of reasoning, he silenced the Sāṅkhyas, and by two, the followers of Yoga.
The distinction from the liberated [self] mentioned previously at the end of the section is not tenable;
for, since the opponent's [position] alone has been rejected, this objection applies only to the inferential [view]. (61)
Thus ends the section concerning those who rely on inference (Ānumānikādhikaraṇa). || 1 ||

Since the [two] methods of *pāriśeṣya* (exhaustion of other possibilities) and *sthāna* (position) do not exist in the case of the *ajā* sentence, the two principles known as the *camasa* and the *ākhyā* are presented here as counter-examples.
Thus ends the section concerning the cups (Camasādhikaraṇa). 2.

Because there is no other scriptural passage [to support it] and because it contradicts the enumeration of the principles (tattva), the present counter-example is offered to dispel the doubt regarding the view that seeks to include [the elements] within the numerical count. (63)
Thus ends the section concerning the inclusion of the number [of elements]. 3.
"In that [which was previously mentioned]"—the state of being a substratum does not exist;
thus, this counter-example is provided against the objection regarding the theory of causality. (64)
Thus ends the section concerning the nature of causality. || 5 ||
The established conclusion is that, because of the prior context, the connection with being the initiator of initiation and so forth,
and because of the characteristic marks of a living being, the word "jagat" (world) should be understood as referring to the individual soul by way of an exception.
Thus concludes the section concerning the designation of the world. 8.

Otherwise, since the principle known as *upapatti* (logical possibility) is not applicable here, there would be a connection with a counter-example in the interpretation of the sentence due to doubt. (66)
Thus concludes the section on the syntactical connection of sentences (Vākyānvayādhikaraṇa). || 6 ||

For it was stated previously, in the section concerning primordial nature (*prakṛti*), that everything arises from both causes; having properly raised an objection to that, the final determination is now made. (67)
Thus ends the section concerning the primordial nature (prakṛti). 7.
In all cases, one should infer for oneself the resolution according to the manner already stated;
thus, all the principles previously mentioned are extended here by analogy. (68)
Thus, this section consisting of eight topics, joined with two groups, reached its conclusion in the fourth quarter of the first chapter. (69)
Thus ends the section concerning the explanation of all [scriptural passages]. || 8 ||
Now, in the two chapters on Non-contradiction (Avirodha), the first two quarters have refuted contradiction based on causes, while the subsequent two have refuted contradiction based on effects. (70)

In the first [section], there shall be a pair of caskets; by means of both [the first two] and by means of the eight systems, as well as through tradition and reasoning, the contradiction that has arisen is gradually resolved. (71)
When there is a desire for a comprehensive elaboration that encompasses all possible explanations,
the principle of Smṛti is applied by way of setting aside the Sāṅkhya Smṛti.
Thus concludes the section concerning Smṛti (tradition). || 1 ||
But regarding the denial of the mindfulness of yoga, there is an application of the previous reasoning;
thus, the connection [of this section] is one based on extended application (ātideśika), as it concerns the refutation of yoga. (73)
Thus ends the section concerning the refutation of Yoga. 2.
In the section concerning "having different characteristics," the Sāṅkhya, relying upon reasoning (*tarka*), opposes [the Buddhist position] once again;
therefore, there is a connection by way of an objection (*ākṣepasaṅgati*). (74)

In the system of "Not Being Accepted by the Learned" (Śiṣṭāparigraha), those [objections] such as Yoga and others which are established through reasoning are refuted by way of extension (atideśa); however, the connection [between the two sections] is one based on that extension.
Thus ends the section concerning what is not accepted by the learned (Śiṣṭāparigrahādhikaraṇa). || 4 ||

Since all rebirths have previously been produced through the state of identifying the body with the self, there arises the refutation of their distinctness and the emergence of the principle of the eater (the enjoyer). 76.
Thus ends the section concerning the identity with the enjoyer (Bhoktrāpatty-adhikaraṇa). || 5 ||
Because of the acceptance of the theory that the effect is non-existent [prior to its production], there is a difference between the cause and the effect;
thus, the section on "Origin" (Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa) serves to refute such objections. || 77 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the originative material cause (Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa). || 6 ||
If there were non-difference in every respect, then the Lord would be a non-Lord; thus, this objection has been refuted by the reasoning immediately following. (78)
Thus ends the section concerning the designation of the other. (Sūtra 7)
The difference [between the two] has been established by means of [attributes] such as "having true desires" (satyakāmatva); the objection that this is not tenable is what is being refuted here. (79)
Thus ends the section concerning the observation of the withdrawal [of the world]. || 8 ||

Milk, water, and so forth, which possess parts, are accepted as being partless Brahman; this is the connection [of the present topic] as a counter-example to the discussion on the consequence of total pervasion (kṛtsnaprasakti). 80.
Thus concludes the section concerning the consequence of the whole [of Brahman] being affected. 9.
"Without a purpose, the Lord cannot create such a diverse world"—this is the objection raised against the theory of purpose (prayojana-naya). (81)
Thus concludes the section on "Possession of a Purpose" (prayojanavattva).
In this manner, within the second and subsequent pādas, ten sections hidden within two sub-sections have been sequentially reconciled with one another. (82)
Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter.
In this way, the contradiction has been avoided; now, in the second quarter [of the verse], the counter-argument is refuted in order to eliminate the doubt of a bystander. (83)
"If the activity of consciousness is fruitless, then it is better that such [activity] belong to the insentient";
this doubt is here refuted by the fact that [such] arrangement is impossible [for the insentient]. (84)
Thus concludes the section on the impossibility of formation.
It might be argued that the world must arise from atoms presided over by a Lord;
this objection regarding the production of the large and the long is now answered. (85)
Thus ends the section concerning the large and the long. || 85 ||
In the doctrine of aggregation, the fault of the theory of origination does not exist;
and this very doubt is also refuted within the system of the collection. (86)
Thus concludes the section concerning the collective whole (samudāyādhikaraṇa). || 3 ||
If that external object exists as something vast, then the aforementioned fault would follow;
therefore, the doctrine of non-existence is presented as a counter-example. (87)
Thus ends the section on perception (upalabdhyadhikaraṇa). 4.
For indeed, no fault whatsoever attaches to the doctrine of universal non-existence;
such is the Madhyamika position, as it is consistent with the application of counter-examples. (88)
Thus ends the section [5] on the impossibility in every respect.
Now, having accepted the removal of all defects through the doctrine of universal selfhood (sārvātmyavāda),
there follows a counter-example arising from the perspective of the Jaina follower.
Thus concludes the section on the impossibility [of coexistence] in a single [locus]. || 6 ||
"Let it be accepted that the entire *pāṃśupata* system is a source of [unwanted] possibilities";
thus, because of the possibility of such doubt, a counter-example is also provided here. (90)
Thus ends the section concerning Paśupati (Sūtra 7).

If the authority of the Pāñcarātra is set aside on the grounds of its similarity to [other] Tantras, then the principle of the impossibility of [the Lord's] origination establishes its authority. (91)
Thus concludes the section on the impossibility of origination (Utpattyasambhavādhikaraṇa). || 8 ||
Thus, the section on the eight topics (aṣṭādhikaraṇī), containing two sub-sections (peṭikā),
reached its conclusion within the Tarkapāda of the Śārīraka [Mīmāṃsā].
Thus ends the summary of the verses.
Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter. || 2 ||
Thus, with all objections set aside, the status of Brahman as the cause is established;
likewise, the status of the world as the effect remains uncontradicted for both [the Sāṅkhya and Vaiśeṣika] systems. (93)
In this [work], both pairs of quarters are characterized as two caskets:
the first consists of seven topical sections (adhikaraṇas), and the second consists of eight perspectives (nayās).
It was stated previously that the discourse on the origination of the living being (jīva) is figurative;
likewise, the doctrine of the origination of space (viyat) is refuted as being similar. 95.
Thus ends the section concerning ether (viyad-adhikaraṇa). || 1 ||
"But the state of being an immediate effect of Brahman would not apply to fire, water, and so forth.
Thus, in the section concerning fire (tejo'dhikaraṇa), this doubt is once again set aside. (96)
Thus ends the section on the superiority of splendor. || 2 ||

Because of the doubt that, by the reasoning previously stated, the individual soul (jīva) might also be an effect, the section concerning the Self (Ātmādhikaraṇa) is reached through the connection known as an exception (apavāda). || 97 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the self (ātman). 3.

Since the nature of the soul, which consists of knowledge, is established as being unproduced, even its transformation into something else would entail the emergence of a substratum for cognition. (98)
Thus ends the section on knowledge (jñādhikaraṇa). 4.
When agency is negated in the Self—which consists solely of the essence of the quality of knowledge and is changeless—then the doctrine of the agent arises. (99)
Thus ends the section concerning the agent (kartradhikaraṇa). 5.
"Agency ceases precisely through the cessation of autonomy"; in order to resolve this objection, the doctrine of dependence on another arises. (100)
Thus ends the section concerning dependence on another (Parāyattādhikaraṇa).

And since dependence on another precludes being a part of that other in the act of agency, this objection having been raised, there now follows the refutation and the re-establishment of the subject as a constituent part. (101)
Thus ends the section concerning the portions (Aṃśādhikaraṇa). || 7 ||
In this case, there would be an extension (atideśa) of the very section concerning the Self;
therefore, the connection with the section concerning the vital breaths (prāṇa) is one based on such extension. || 103 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the origin of the vital breaths (Prāṇa). || 1 ||
Thus, having stated the functional nature of the sense organs as a consequence, there shall now be a consideration of their number according to the principle of the sevenfold course. || 104 ||
Thus ends the section on the seven destinies. 2.
In this context, the nature of the sense organs and the vital breaths (prāṇas) is now considered;
in the section concerning the atomicity of the prāṇas, it is established that they are atomic when their functions expand. (105)
Thus concludes the section on the atomicity of the vital breaths (prāṇa). 4.

Because there are many disputes even regarding the true nature of the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa), the determination of that reality follows as a corollary in the section concerning air and its functions. 106.
Thus ends the section concerning the functions of air (vāyu). 4.
The fact that the *śreṣṭha-prāṇa* is an effect and its essential nature have been described;
furthermore, its atomicity (*aṇutva*) has also been explained incidentally in the section concerning the atomicity of the *śreṣṭha*. (107)
Thus ends the section concerning the minuteness of the soul (Śeṣṭhāṇutvādhikaraṇa). || 5 ||
The limited quantity of the vital breaths is established through the discussion of their measurement;
furthermore, the presiding deities, such as Agni and others, are considered therein. (108)
Thus ends the section concerning the presiding over light and so forth (Jyotirādyadhiṣṭhānādhikaraṇa).

Since deliberation [on the senses] would be fruitless if they were not distinguished from the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the presentation of the method of the senses (*indriyanaya*) arises for the purpose of resolving this objection. (109)
Thus ends the section concerning the sense-faculties (indriya-adhikaraṇa). 7.
The Supreme Self alone must be the cause in the creation of the collective whole;
however, in the case of the individual triad of name and form, that [causality] is set aside in favor of the individual soul.
Thus ends the section concerning the fashioning of names and forms (Saṃjñāmūrtiklṛptyadhikaraṇa).
Dispassion, both types of goodness, the marks [of a yogi], and knowledge as well as ignorance—these are considered the primary subjects of the first four quarters of the third chapter. (111)
The discussion regarding the body has already been conducted here concerning the perception of another body;
now, in this subsequent section, the conjunction with the subtle elements is being examined. (112)
Thus ends the section concerning the attainment of the intermediate state. 1.

Now, according to the principle of "one who has only one more birth" (*ekabhavika*), when the remainder of karma is eliminated, the connection of what remains after being experienced is declared by the *kṛtātyayanyāya*. (113)
Thus ends the section concerning the passing away [of those who have performed works]. || 2 ||

Having previously raised the doubt that the path of the moon belongs to those who perform sacrifices, works of public utility, and acts of charity, this [path] is now denied for those who perform undesirable deeds and the like.
Thus ends the section concerning those who perform undesirable actions and so forth. || 3 ||

For those who perform sacrifices and other rites and descend from the moon, there occurs a refinement into the state of water and so forth, according to the principle of attaining the nature of that [substance]. (115)
Thus ends the section concerning the attainment of that very nature. 4.

An investigation into whether [the process] takes a long or short time was conducted regarding the state of being a cloud and so forth, according to the principle of "not very long," for the purpose of establishing the suffering of living beings. (116)
Thus ends the section concerning "not too long. 5.

The state of being rice and so forth for living beings who have descended here [into this world] is described as "rice and so forth" when they are embraced by that which is presided over by another. (117)
Thus ends the section concerning that which is presided over by another (Anyādhiṣṭhitādhikaraṇa). || 6 ||
Thus, in the first pāda of the third chapter, the six doctrines are mutually contained within a single section by virtue of their connection through incidental context (prasaṅga). 118.
Thus ends the first quarter of the third chapter. || 1 ||
The living being, though free from the defects of the waking state, remains in the state of dreaming;
the suspicion that it is therefore faultless is refuted by the logic of the twilight period.
Thus ends the section on the twilight devotions (sandhyā). || 1 ||

Whether the individual soul (jīva) in the dream state be defective, or that in the state of deep sleep be free from defects—this very doubt is raised according to the theory of their non-existence [in the waking state]. (120)
Thus concludes the section on the non-existence of that [pradhāna].

Regarding the discussion on the recollection of karma, it is raised as an objection that the individual soul (jīva) alone would be faultless when arising from deep sleep or from any other state; this doubt is now refuted.
Thus ends the section concerning the injunctions regarding words that recall past actions. 3.

The analogy of the "fainting person" (mugdhanyāya) has been introduced in order to establish the abundance of defects in one who exists in the three aforementioned states; therefore, there is a connection by way of introduction (upoddhāta).
Thus ends the section on the deluded person (Mugdhādhikaraṇa). 4.

Now, in this section concerning that which possesses both characteristics (ubhayaliṅgādhikaraṇa), the defect that arose due to the commonality of the Supreme Self with consciousness is here set aside. (123)
Thus concludes the section on the two-fold characteristics (ubhayaliṅgādhikaraṇa). || 5 ||

Thus, for the sake of the purity and purification declared in the *Ahikuṇḍala* method, the nature of the non-conscious as Brahman is stated; therefore, there is a connection by way of introduction (*upoddhāta*).
Thus ends the section concerning the serpent and its coils (Ahikuṇḍalādhikaraṇa).

"The ultimate cause of the proliferation of conceptual elaboration (prapañca) is held to be the pure reality (tattva)"—thus did the Proponent of the Ultimate (paramanaya) cut through this objection. (125)
Thus ends the section concerning another [subject]. || 7 ||

When an action yields its fruit, the worship of the cause [of that action] would then be useless; in order to pacify this objection, the Giver of the fruit is declared to be the triad of causes. (126)
Thus, this section on the eight topics, adorned by two caskets,
is well-integrated with one another in this second quarter of the third chapter.
Thus ends the section on the fruit (phalādhikaraṇa). || 8 ||
In the context of the Lord granting fruits when pleased by worship, there is an investigation into His difference and non-difference for the sake of practical application in ritual performance. (128)

This is because of the combination of the arguments stated in the section concerning other recensions (śākhāntarādhikaraṇa), and because of the principle of all Vedāntas applying to that Vaiśvānara-vidyā and others. (129)
Thus concludes the section [establishing] that [Brahman] is the subject matter of all Vedānta texts. 1.
Now, in this section concerning "alteration," just as in the previous case of Vaiśvānara, the unity of the meditations on the Udgītha is likewise set aside. (130)
Thus ends the section on changeability (Anyathātvādhikaraṇa). || 2 ||

In the section concerning the non-difference of all [meditations], the doubt regarding a difference in the *prāṇa*-vidyās is set aside because of the injunction of a difference in form, owing to their being included therein. (131)
Thus ends the section concerning the non-difference of all.

"The knowledge of the Truths (Satyādi-vidyā) would be distinct because of the difference in its ritual procedure and form"—this doubt is refuted in the Ānandana school by means of its essential nature (svarūpa). (132)
Thus ends the section concerning Ānanda and others. 4.

In the section concerning the description of the effects (kāryākhyānādhikaraṇa), he states that the meditation on the abode of the vital breaths is restricted, due to the similarity with the reasoning of the preceding section. 133.
Thus concludes the section concerning the accomplishment of the task (Kāryākhyānādhikaraṇa). || 5 ||
Moreover, even when there is a common substratum, a difference in knowledge is set aside on account of the conceit of a difference in form; for [powers] such as mastery are indeed included within it.
Thus ends the section on grammatical coreferentiality (samānādhikaraṇa). || 6 ||

Now, in the section concerning the connection [between the two Upaniṣads], the doubt that the knowledge of the eye and the sun is identical—arising from the conceit of a difference in form—is set aside on account of the difference in location. (135)
Thus ends the section concerning the relationship [of the subordinate]. || 7 ||
The objection that, because there is no distinction of location for the two powers of accumulation and governance, their pervasion must be omnipresent, is now addressed. (136)
Thus ends the section concerning the materials for the sacrificial fire (Sambhṛtyadhikaraṇa). || 8 ||

The section concerning the knowledge of the Person (puruṣavidyā) declares that the Yājñavalkya version of this knowledge—due to mere proximity—is a subordinate part of the higher knowledge (paravidyā), because of its similarity to it. (137)
Thus ends the section concerning the knowledge of the Person (Puruṣavidyā). || 9 ||

Now, regarding the eligibility for piercing and other rites, the status as auxiliary members of the mantras beginning with "śukram" is raised as a doubt and then refuted through the effort prescribed for the male [initiate] and the Vidyā.
Thus ends the section concerning piercing and so forth (Adhikaraṇa 10).
Just as it was previously stated that [the subsidiary nature] exists in the case of the production of the *hāni* and so forth due to the remainder of the ritual action (*karmaśeṣatā*),
in the same way, there is a mutual subsidiarity (*anyonyaśeṣatā*) based on the mark (*liṅga*) of the inherent capacity of the entities.
Thus ends the section concerning the other [deities].
In the section concerning the future state (samparāya), the reflection on abandonment and attainment is established;
because of the extraction of the time [of death], there is thus a connection as an introductory topic (upoddhāta). || 140 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the state after death (Sāmparāyādhikaraṇa). || 12 ||

In the same way, if the principle of non-restriction were applied, then all [beings] would have the path beginning with the Archis as their destination; thus, the previously established doctrines would be contradicted. || 141 ||
Thus concludes the section on the lack of fixed rule (aniyamādhikaraṇa). 13.

Now, just as there is a connection with the path beginning with light (arcir-ādi-gati) for those engaged in meditation on the Imperishable (akṣara), so too there would be a connection with the meditations on the Imperishable; such is the application of the illustrative example. || 142 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the syllable *akṣara*. 14.

Because Brahman is free from anything to be abandoned and because functions such as breathing are impossible [for Him], the doubt that He might be the individual soul (jīva) is dispelled in the section concerning the "Inner One" (Antaratva-adhikaraṇa). || 143 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning internality (Antaratvādhikaraṇa). || 15 ||
The doubt that "if one has mastery over desire and so forth, then by the previous reasoning, [qualities] such as mastery would be restricted" is also refuted here. (144)
Thus ends the section concerning desire and so forth (Kāmādyadhikaraṇa). || 16 ||
By the principle of specific determination (*nirdhāraṇanyāya*), and due to doubts dependent on prior reasoning, even the restriction regarding the meditations on the *udgītha* is set aside. (145)
Thus ends the section concerning the rules for the concentration on that [Brahman]. 17.
Since the previous legal case has arrived as a rebuttal (apavāda), there shall be a legal case concerning the giving [of the girl], following the remainder of the section on desire (kāma). || 146 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the giving [of the sacrificial fee]. 18.

Previously, when the unity of all Vidyās was established by the force of the method [of interpretation], any doubt regarding it was dispelled by the statement in the section on the "Abundance of Indicative Marks" (Liṅgabhūyastva). || 147 ||
Thus concludes the section on the abundance of indicative marks (liṅgabhūyastva). || 19 ||
Since there is no statement of refutation, a doubt arising from the context is countered once again by means of the principle known as the "prior alternative" (pūrvavikalpa). || 148 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the prior conceptualization (pūrvavikalpādhikaraṇa). || 20 ||
Then, due to the intensity of proximity, there arises a contemplation of its form at that very time;
subsequently, this is projected upon the worshiper's body through the process of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā).
Thus ends the section concerning the existence [of the soul] in the body. || 21 ||

Moreover, even though there is an excellence of proximity based on the established conclusion of the preceding section, the connection with the entire *udgītha* would occur according to the principle of being bound to the subordinate parts (*aṅga*). (150)
Thus concludes the section on those [rites] connected with the limbs (aṅgāvabaddha). || 22 ||
By the same logic applied to the meditation on the Udgītha, even in the case of the Vaiśvānara doctrine,
the doubt regarding the totality and its parts is set aside by the principle of the "Great One" (bhūman).
Thus ends the section concerning the superiority of the "Great" (bhūman). || 23 ||

In the section concerning various sounds (*nānāśabdādhikaraṇa*), following the method of the Vaiśvānara section, the suspicion that the cognitions of the heart, the eyes, and so forth are identical is set aside. (152)
Thus ends the section concerning the distinction based on words and other factors.

In the systematic arrangement of the different branches of knowledge, there is an exception to the combination [of all practices] for a single qualified practitioner, just as there is a restriction regarding alternatives. || 153 ||
Thus ends the section on conceptual construction (vikalpādhikaraṇa). || 25 ||

The doubt as to whether there is a restrictive rule for the meditation on the *udgītha* or a rule of optionality is here dispelled by the principle of "according to the substrate" (*yathāśrayanyāya*). (154)
Thus, in this third chapter and also in its third section, the connection of twenty-six topics has been fully illustrated. (155)
Thus ends the section concerning the existence [of qualities] according to their substrata. 26.
In the section on the limbs (aṅga), there is a systematic arrangement of fifteen topics of inquiry according to four, seven, two, and two principles respectively. (156)
Unlike the meditation on the *udgītha*, the attainment of Brahman is not held to be for the sake of the ritual;
this constitutes a counter-example in connection with the section concerning the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). (157)
Thus concludes the section concerning the human goal (puruṣārtha).

Even though the two passages concerning the stages of life lack the status of being explanatory eulogies (*arthavāda*) for the state of being established in Brahman, a doubt arises that they might be eulogies for the *udgītha*, which is resolved by the principle of praise. (158)
Thus concludes the section concerning mere praise (stutimātrādhikaraṇa). || 2 ||

The doubt that "the rule for the Pāriplava [narratives] would be like the rule for the Udgītha and Upastīva" is here set aside by the established principle that they are for the purpose of knowledge (vidyā). 159.
Thus concludes the section concerning the meaning of the *pāriplava*. 3.
When one is established in the state of a wandering mendicant, two logical principles apply regarding the tendency toward praise:
the doubt that ritual action is not an auxiliary factor must be set aside, according to the principle of the fire and the fuel. (160)
Thus ends the section concerning the kindling of the fires and the bringing of the sacrificial materials. 4.

"The objection that this knowledge would be independent of sacrifices, like the practice of lighting a fire with fuel, is now refuted by the principle of the dependence on all [means] (sarvāpekṣā). (161)
Thus ends the section concerning the dependence on all [works]. || 5 ||

Even for a householder, if knowledge is attained through tranquility, self-control, and so forth, any suspicion that tranquility and the like are not auxiliary factors [to that knowledge] is dispelled by the rule of calming [the mind]. (162)
Thus ends the section concerning tranquility, self-control, and so forth. || 6 ||
"The knowledge of the vital breaths (prāṇavidyā) does not require restraint regarding the scope of food"—by this principle of permission for all kinds of food, the doubt has been dispelled. (163)
Thus ends the section concerning the permission to eat all food (sarvānnānumati). || 7 ||
Thus, if all karma is completed within knowledge for the wise, then for others there is the censure of acting according to one's own will, because [action] has been prescribed [as a duty]. (164)
Thus ends the section concerning that which is prescribed. || 8 ||

"If one who is not in an āśrama were not entitled [to perform rites] because the duties of the āśramas are auxiliary to knowledge (vidyā),"—this objection is now refuted; furthermore, there are those who [perform them] even in the interval between āśramas. (165)
Thus ends the section concerning the one who is destitute [of a teacher]. || 9 ||
"There might still be eligibility even for those who have fallen after having ascended"—this doubt regarding the *tadbhūtākhyāna* rite is dispelled by the scriptural statement. (166)
Thus ends the section concerning that which has come into being (tadbhūtādhikaraṇa). || 10 ||
"In the meditation on the Udgītha, a priest should not be authorized because of the mention of the fruit [of the rite];
this objection is now refuted incidentally upon the determination of the master's entitlement. (167)
Thus concludes the section on ownership (svāmyadhikaraṇa). 11.
Meditation (manana) is considered another auxiliary factor because it is not in conflict with karma;
its connection with the preceding section on the five means (pañcamanaya), however, is by way of exception (āpavādika).
Thus concludes the section concerning the injunction for another auxiliary means. || 22 ||

Because it is contrary to knowledge and ritual action, childhood is not at all accepted as a constituent part [of the path]; thus there is a refutation of the objection based on the principle of non-manifestation. 169.
Thus ends the section concerning non-disclosure (anāviṣkārādhikaraṇa). 13.

"Karma is not a constituent part [of the means], because there is deviation in the case of worship performed for the sake of enjoyment"—this objection is refuted here by the principle of "belonging to this world" (*aihika*). (170)
Thus ends the section concerning the present life (Aihikādhikaraṇa). || 14 ||
Thus, the principle stated regarding meditation on the fruit of liberation is extended [by analogy] here;
consequently, there is generally no fixed rule, as a powerful obstacle usually exists. (171)
Thus ends the section concerning the fruit of liberation (Muktiphalādhikaraṇa). || 15 ||
Thus, having occupied the third [section], the fifteenth *adhikriyā*, which is well-integrated and governs many mixed [cases], resides in the fourth quarter. 172.
Thus ends the fourth quarter.
Now, these are considered the principal subjects of the quarters of the fourth chapter:
conjunction [with the subtle body], departure, the path, and the attainment of the Supreme Brahman. (173)
In the first two feet there are two caskets:
one is the Vidya-vishodhini, and the other is the Phala-bodhini, consisting of six maxims and five maxims respectively. (174)
But if the meaning of the treatise were established all at once, what would be the point of considering its completion?
It is to refute such an objection that the possibility of the principle of repetition (āvṛtti-nyāya) arises. (175)
Thus ends the section concerning repetition (āvṛttyadhikaraṇa). || 1 ||

To refute the objection—"If the Self is always manifest directly, what is this [notion] of being accomplished through the removal of obscuration?"—there is the qualification regarding the eligibility for the meditation on the nature of the Self. (176)
Thus ends the section concerning the meditation on the Self. 2.
If the knowledge taught in the Upaniṣads consists of worship in the form of identifying [the object] with one's own self,
then this same objection is also removed in the case of the worship of symbols (pratīka).
Thus ends the section concerning the Pratīkas. 3.
It has been stated that it is logical to view the superior in what is inferior;
here, however, the doubt regarding viewing the Udgītha in the sun and so forth is set aside.
Thus concludes the section concerning the meditation on [the breath] as the sun and so forth. || 4 ||
If it were held that meditation must be repeated at will, then there would be the objection that [the result] could be achieved by repetition;
however, this is refuted by the fact that the qualification for meditation applies to one who is already seated [in the practice]. (179)
Thus ends the section concerning one who is seated. 5.
The doubt as to whether one who has returned [to worldly life] may also withdraw [from it] at their own will is refuted in the *Āprayāṇādhikaraṇa* by the observation of scriptural evidence. (180)
Thus concludes the section concerning [the soul's state] until the departure from the body (āprayāṇādhikaraṇa). 6.
Furthermore, the objection that even meditation performed until the end of life lacks the opportunity to yield its fruit due to the infinity of past sins is thereby refuted. (181)
Thus ends the section concerning the realization of that [Brahman]. 7.
Now, in the subsequent section, although merit is infinite as before, these two—destruction and non-attachment—apply respectively to the sphere of accidental evil action and virtuous action. (182)
Thus ends the section concerning the other [deity]. 8.
Likewise, it is established that [the two types of karma] have as their objects only those [deeds] not yet begun;
thus, the objection that there would be no contradiction with direct perception is pacified. || 183 ||
Thus ends the section concerning those whose karma has not yet begun to bear fruit. 9.

"If there were no connection even with well-performed deeds, then acting according to one's own whims would follow as a consequence"—this objection is indeed refuted by the principle of the Agnihotra sacrifice once again. (184)
Thus ends the section concerning the Agnihotra. 10.

Regarding the objection that the destruction of *prārabdha* karma occurs through good deeds such as the *agnihotra*, this is refuted by the established principle that [the exhaustion of *prārabdha*] must end only with experience (*bhoga*). || 185 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the destruction of others. 11.
Thus, in the first quarter (pāda) of the fourth chapter, there is a summary of the connections between the eleven principles in their proper order. (186)
Thus ends the first quarter of the fourth chapter. 1.
In this regard, there should be two baskets (peṭikā) consisting of seven and four principles respectively, which have as their scope the general course and the specific course in due order. (187)

The reflection on the sequence of speech and other faculties is intended to refute the objection that there may be a delay in the fruit even at the end of prārabdha karma when the departure [of the soul] is not fixed. (188)
Thus ends the section concerning speech. || 1 ||
Thereafter, the section concerning the mind (manas) is introduced as a counter-example;
all of that is now considered, for it is to be contemplated by yogis because it is preceded by its fruit. (189)
Thus ends the section concerning the mind (manas). || 2 ||

Having understood the scriptural sequence (śrauta-krama) previously stated, since the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) is possible, the emergence of the system of direct perception (adhyakṣa-naya) occurs through the connection of an exception (āpavādika-saṅgati). || 190 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the superintendent. 3.
Since the prima facie argument arises from taking the meaning exactly as it was heard,
the doubt raised even in the section concerning the elements (Bhūtādhikaraṇa) has been refuted.
Thus ends the section concerning the elements (bhūtādhikaraṇa). 4.

Since it is clearly stated in the sacred tradition that "the wise one attains Brahman here," the investigation into the principle of the river-current (āsṛtinyāya) is intended to resolve the doubt raised by the [apparent] contradiction regarding departure [from the body]. 192.
Thus ends the section concerning the commencement of the course of transmigration (Āsṛtyupakramādhikaraṇa). || 5 ||

The qualification for the supreme attainment is established solely for the purpose of conceiving a fruit, so as to dispel the objection that resting in the midst of the departure would be fruitless. (193)
Thus ends the section on the excellence of others. 6.

Thinking, "There will be only dejection toward sentient beings who possess excellence," this determination of the method of non-differentiation is for the purpose of removing such doubts and objections. (194)
Thus ends the section on non-differentiation (Avibhāgādhikaraṇa). || 7 ||
When the channel (nāḍī) is difficult to distinguish even when the destination (gati) is common, the doubt arising from its lack of necessity is removed by this rule. || 195 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the abode (tadoko'dhikaraṇa).

"Because there is an absence of rays during the night, the consideration of the movement is inconceivable"—this objection and refutation also falls within the scope of the reasoning concerning the secondary rays. (196)
Thus ends the section concerning the following of the rays. || 9 ||
While the splendors of the suns are present, the setting of the night is intended here to counteract the objection based on the defect of time. (197)
Thus ends the section concerning the night. 10.
However, because reaching the moon is possible during the southern course, the determination of the southern course is for the sake of remaining in the state of cessation. || 198 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning the southern solstice (Dakṣiṇāyana). || 11 ||
Thus, in the second section (caraṇa) of the fourth chapter as well, the sections concerning the protection of the intermediate space between the two enclosures have been concluded. (199)
Thus ends the second quarter of the fourth chapter.

Even when the defects of time have been pacified, if the path of light (arciradhvan) is not established, there is no attainment of liberation due to distraction; thus, the constant removal of that [distraction] is the "light" (arciḥ). || 200 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the Path beginning with Light (Arcirādy-adhikaraṇa). || 1 ||

Even when contradictions between the branches [of the Veda] have been resolved, the application of the principle of air (vāyunyāya) arises to refute the distraction caused by internal alternatives. // 201 //
Thus ends the section concerning the air (vāyvadhikaraṇa). 2.
In this same way, even the ritual authority over Varuṇa dispels internal doubt;
likewise, the meditation on the path beginning with light (arcirādi) as a limb of yoga is free from all obstacles.
Thus concludes the section concerning Varuṇa. 3.
Even in the doctrine of the subtle body (ātivāhika), there is likewise a shaking of the subject matter;
whether it be an objection or a refutation, let the connection be determined. (203)
Thus ends the section concerning the subtle body (the *ātivāhika*). 4.

Although the *ātivāhika* body has been determined, and the *ativāha* (the conductors) have been established, the section concerning the *kārya* (the effect) arises in order to pacify the objection regarding its purposelessness. (204)
Thus ends the section concerning the effect (kāryādhikaraṇa). 5.
In the fourth chapter, in its fourth quarter, adorned with two sections, liberation and sovereignty are described through the division into triads and dyads for the sake of liberation. (206)
If liberation is the manifestation of one's true nature, then even deep sleep would be such;
the futility of contemplating the path and so forth has been refuted by the principle of "attainment" (sampannīti).
Thus concludes the section concerning the manifestation [of the soul] upon the attainment [of Brahman]. || 1 ||

According to the principle of non-distinction, because the determination of the meaning of the essential nature [of the Self] has been established, the connection [with the present topic] can be understood through the method of introduction (upoddhāta). 208.
Thus ends the section concerning the perception [of Brahman] as non-differentiated. 9.
Furthermore, the method regarding the section on Brahman has already been explained previously;
the connection has also been stated, for that triad indeed constitutes a single chapter (peṭikā). (209)
Thus ends the section concerning Brahmā. || 3 ||
Thus, when sovereignty consists of all enjoyments for one who is liberated, this objection—that cyclic existence would occur in turn—is thereby refuted. || 210 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the resolve (saṅkalpa). 4.
Sovereignty, characterized by the desire for non-obstruction and awakened through the method of resolve, generally purifies internal afflictions according to the subsequent principle. (211)
Thus ends the section concerning non-existence (abhāvādhikaraṇa). || 5 ||
"If there were an absence of activity toward the world, His perfection would be limited"—this objection is refuted by the principle of the Lord's engagement with the world. (212)
Thus, the six systems of logic have come together in this fourth quarter, which defines the Turya state and is intent upon ascertaining the essence of the scriptures—may it be auspicious! (213)
This garland of harmonious compositions, filled with the flowers of the Master’s eloquent verses, consists of one hundred and fifty-six topical sections. 214.
The Lord of Śrī, having accepted this garland of the systematic arrangement of principles determined in the *Śrībhāṣya*, rejoiced. || 215 ||
This *Mālā* was compiled for the delight of those desiring to collect [the teachings] by the sovereign scholar Śrīnivāsa at Lakṣmīpura. 216.
Thus ends the *Nayasaṃgatimālikā*.
Thus concludes the section [beginning with] "Excluding the Activity of the World" (Jagadvyāpāravarjādhikaraṇa). 6.
